# Introduction

## Background

This project addresses the problem of creative burnout and lack of motivation for both starting and finishing creative projects. Many are frustrated with their perceived inability to finish projects or feel overwhelmed by the prospect of some ideas that seem too large. Others find it difficult to begin projects in the first place, pointing to a lack of ideas, motivation, a fear of failure and intimidation (among other reasons). MakeUp is an app that provides users with bite-sized creative prompts and a competition system in order to encourage users to both start smaller novel projects and to encourage users to consistently finish projects that motivate them to continue creating rather than uninstalling the app or quitting creative projects altogether.

It has been found that a moderate level of competition can increase both creative productivity and originality (@Gross2020). If a creative actor has is faced with a challenge that they perceive as too difficult, they will abandon the project that they were going to produce, meaning that this creative work will never be shared with the rest of the world. If the competition is perceived as too easy, however, the subject will not be motivated to create a project with a high degree of originality. Because of the low bar set by low competition, much of competitors' output will be very similar to each other. MakeUp features a dynamic competition system that adapts to the user's level of creative activity. If a user is consistently submitting projects and collecting higher point totals per day and week, the competition will increase in difficulty in order to motivate the user to continue completing prompts in the app. If a user is struggling to submit projects regularly due to time constraints or lack of motivation, or uninstalled the app but is reinstalling it during a burst of motivation, the competition will ease the user into the app by providing a less punishing competitive environment. This will hopefully discourage users from uninstalling the app within a day or two, pushing their motivational satellite into an orbit rather than a crash to the ground (only to be launched unsuccessfully again at a later date).

MakeUp also is designed to help the user form habits when tackling creative projects by emphasizing convenience. Apps are a unique tool in that they are readily available for a large portion of the population. About 91% of Americans own a smartphone, including about 96% of American adults under 50 years of age (@SmartphoneOwnership). Apps are accessible to most to use in the first place and are also staring users in the face when they record their average screen time of roughly 5 hours per day (@Alam2023). Conveniency is king when forming habits: businesses that have launched mobile apps have generally seen an increase in their sales figures due to the formation of habitual interaction with brands (@VanHeerde2019). The potential for apps to help users form desired habits is also evident for students. Students who used a mobile app to intentionally track their habits over just 6 weeks were able to significantly increase the automaticity of their desired behaviors as well as limit their motivational impairments (@Stojanovic2020). It is clear that an app is one of the most powerful tools that could be implemented to help users form habits; MakeUp uses the convenience of app accessibility and visibility in order form patterns of consistent creative output.

## Overview of MakeUp

MakeUp is an android application that uses a point system and prompts to encourage users to submit bite-sized creative projects to the app every day. Users are given three daily prompts at midnight each day: a one-point, two-point and three-point prompt (the amount of points should correlate roughly to the time commitment required for a project). The user can choose one of the three prompts each day to complete and submit to the app. These prompts should be able to be completed in a short amount of time; one-point prompts should be completable in about 10 minutes, two-point prompts in about 20 minutes, and three-point prompts in about 30 minutes. Prompt submissions will be uploaded to the user's profile page, which displays all past file and text submissions so that the user can see tangible results. Users who can more easily see the measurable progress that they have made using the app will be more likely to gain a positive perception of their work (@Amabile2007).

Similarly, users are able to complete a weekly prompt that is submitted to their profile page. The difference, however, is that rather than the weekly prompt being assigned each week, the user is required to submit their own prompt or goal to the app and assign it its own point value (capped at 15 points). This allows users who benefit more from a journaling workstyle to set their own goals and track their progress through the profile page, which displays both completed weekly prompts and past weekly prompt ideas that were never finished. The weekly prompt also safeguards users from an overreliance on prompts which are not original to them. While the daily prompts can be a great source of inspiration and helpful for bite-sized projects, the trade-off is that users may not diverge much from what they see others doing for similar projects because the base idea for the project is not their own. Additionally, the daily prompt is limited in that the user may not necessarily love the three ideas that they are given each day. The weekly prompt gives users an outlet to create their own projects from scratch and explore more niche projects that may not be included in the app's daily prompts (both on a specific day or generally). Summarized, the daily prompt is a powerful tool for kickstarting the creative process and providing inspiration for more easily completable projects with quickly visible results, while the weekly prompt should be harnessed to provide flexibility within the app's experience and to encourage users to flex their creative muscles in a more personal way.

The component of the app that helps to motivate users in their quest for increased creative output is the "League" system. Users are placed on a leaderboard with rival non-human competitors. The user then accumulates points over a four week period or "season" by completing daily and weekly prompts. This accumulation of points or lack therof causes the user to rise or fall on the leaderboard. If a user places above a certain threshold on the leaderboard, they will be promoted to a higher league. If they place below a certain threshold, they will be relegated to a lower league.

## Ethical Implications

- MakeUp will be entirely local, so creative projects will not be stored by the creators of the app. This will mitigate privacy concerns and potential misuse of data.
- Though MakeUp does not have an online competition element, people may still compare their points totals and try to boost their points through their weekly prompts (and in the process, misuse the tool). This could also cause unhealthy competition between users.
    - Point caps on weekly prompts will help marginalize this issue.
- People could become overly reliant on the creative prompts given by the app instead of making their own creative projects.
    - The weekly prompts are user-created so that users are still creating their own content and ideas.
    - The app will have a very large database of prompts so that users come across a large variety of prompts.

## Key contributions

- MakeUp is an app that encourages users to consistentally create bite-sized projects rather than burning out or becoming overwhelmed by larger projects.
- MakeUp also features a dynamic competition element that both eases in users that have not submitted a project in a while and also challenges more competitive users who have been consistently submitting projects.
    - The goal should be moderate competition that challenges users slightly but does not feel overly uncomfortable.
- MakeUp was tested by timing different elements in an efficient way that doesn't slow down the app meaningfully.
